age_band.note: No birth date in the sources read; an educated interpreter in the service since before 1808, drawn at about forty. The skeleton Kirkland thought his was of a man of "complete maturity" (Dr. Freer).

present_on_scene_date.note: Dead since 17 June; not in the 14 August scene. No source takes a roll call on the afternoon of 14 August 1812; this is read from the evidence below.

persons.note: The government's interpreter at Fort Dearborn, a Frenchman with a house on the north side of the river. He was killed just outside the fort's entrance on the evening of 17 June 1812, in a fight with John Kinzie. In the town from 1803-10-01 to 1812-06-17: He wintered 1803-04 at Chicago with Dr. Smith (Quaife; the month is ours) and was killed at sunset on 17 June 1812 (Van Voorhis and Irwin as the Reader quotes them; Quaife: after 13 April). The Reader reports a deed of 1800 that has him buy du Sable's post, which would put him at Chicago earlier.

evidence.quote: For several years before 1812, John Lalime, a Frenchman, had been the government's salaried interpreter at Fort Dearborn.
La Lime was living in one of the four houses on the north side of the river and acting as government Indian interpreter
evidence.claim: his house on the north side and his post

evidence.quote: described him as "a very decent man and a good companion."
An Indian from the Peorias passed here yesterday and has given me information
Lalime's letters show that he was a man of ability and education.
three of the long-time residents of Chicago, La Lime, Ouilmette, and Kinzie, were not included in this number
It could not have been earlier than April 13, however, since on this date he wrote to Captain Wells
La Lime was stabbed to death by Kinzie in a personal encounter just outside the entrance to Fort Dearborn.
